pages.head: The Story
pages.html:
Ohm Sweet Ohm

A logic puzzle in twenty-three circuit boards

In 1995 the Bitmore family of Juniper Lane had the first Smart Home on the block. Every appliance in the house talked to every other appliance: the coffee maker woke the toaster, the toaster warmed up the TV, and the TV told the garage door when the news was over.

Then came the thunderstorm. One bolt of lightning hit the TV antenna, ran down the house wiring and scrambled everything. Now the toaster opens the garage door. The fridge changes the channel. The clock radio plays polka at three in the morning.

Somebody has to fix it. Somebody small.

Watt is a pocket-sized repair robot who lives in the main fuse box, right next to his charging socket. The lightning bounced him clear across the house and into the toaster! To get home, Watt must roll through the circuit board of every haywire appliance - in the kitchen, the living room, the garage and the attic - rewiring as he goes.

Live current will fizzle a little robot in a blink. But current is also the only thing that switches off the force-field gates between Watt and home. Flip the switches, follow the copper, and think before you roll.

There's no place like Ohm!

pages.head: Getting Started
pages.html:
Getting Started

Type OHMSWEET and press Enter. You need a VGA display. A Sound Blaster (or compatible) plays the music and the clack of the switches; without one, the PC speaker beeps along.

A short cartoon shows the storm. Press any key for the menu and pick Play. Leave the menu alone for half a minute and Watt will show you how the first board is done.

Before each board a card shows its name and a picture of it. Press any key (or wait a moment) and Watt drops onto the GND pad in the middle of the board. Somewhere on the board is an outlet: roll onto it and you are through to the next board.

Spare batteries

Watt starts with 9 spare batteries (the F2 screen calls them Lives). Every time he touches live current, or you reboot the board, he uses one up and the board starts over, exactly as it was. Each outlet you reach gives you one more, and so does each gold screw. Run out and the game is over.

Press F5 to save your game between tries and F6 to load it.

pages.head: Controls
pages.html:
Controls

KeyWhat it does
Up W 8Roll up one block
Down S 2Roll down one block
Left A 4Roll left one block
Right D 6Roll right one block
RReboot: start this board over (costs a spare battery)
F1Help
F2Score and spare batteries
F3 / F4Music / sound effects on and off
F5 / F6Save / load a game
EscQuit to the menu

Watt rolls exactly one block for each press of a key, so he is always squarely on the board. There are no diagonal moves: circuit boards are wired in straight lines, and so is Watt.

To work a switch, a timer button or a fuse, just roll into it. You bump it and stay where you are.

pages.head: Current
pages.html:
Current

Batteries sit in the housing at the edge of a board, each one feeding its own copper wire. A steady stream of glowing beads runs out along the wire: that is live current. Touch a bead and Watt fizzles.

Current is not instant. When a switch is turned on, you can watch the current race down the wire, about as fast as Watt can roll. When it is turned off, the last beads still have to run out to the end before the wire is safe.

A wire with no beads on it is dead and perfectly safe to roll over.

Force-field gates

The crackling yellow gates stand between Watt and the outlet. A gate is deadly to touch. But a gate is always at the end of a wire, and the moment current reaches it, the gate shuts down for good. After that its posts soak up any current that follows, so the doorway is safe.

That is the heart of every board: get current to the gates without getting current on Watt.

Kinds of battery

  • Green batteries run steadily, all the time.
  • Pulsing batteries (marked ~) blink on and off, sending current down the wire in bursts with gaps between. Two pulsing batteries often take turns.
  • Dead batteries (marked !) do nothing until Watt bumps them. Then they start, and they never, ever stop.

pages.head: Parts
pages.html:
Parts on the Board

PartWhat it does
Knife switchBump it to flip it. Down (on) lets current through; up (off) stops it. Flip it as often as you like.
Timer buttonBump it and it lets current through for about five seconds, then turns itself off. Watch the clock hand go round.
FuseCarries current until Watt bumps it. Then it blows and its wire is dead forever.
Diode (arrow)Watt can roll through it only the way the arrow points. Once past, there is no going back!
Relay NONormally open. Ordinary current can't get through until pink control current reaches the relay. Then it is thrown, and stays thrown.
Relay NCNormally closed. Ordinary current runs straight through until pink control current reaches it. Then it opens, and stays open.
555 timerA little eight-legged chip that pulses its wire, on a little longer than off (wired the usual way, a 555 is always on longer than off). Its red OUT light goes dark with the current.
LCD screen, CitiCarCurrent lights them up, then runs on through to whatever is next. A blank LCD shows a row of boxes; booted, it says READY.
OutletThe way out. 1,000 points and a spare battery.
Gold screw500 points and a spare battery.

Reading the wires

Copper traces show where every wire goes, even when it is dead, so you can always follow a wire from its battery to its gate. Where two wires cross, one hops over the other on a little bridge: they are not connected. Where a wire runs through the housing it can't hurt Watt, and Watt can't reach the parts there.

Pink control current is ordinary current's bossy big sister: it throws relays, and ordinary current can't cross it.

pages.head: Thinking Like an Electrician
pages.html:
Thinking Like an Electrician

Every board can be solved, and none needs fast fingers: a little patience and a little planning will do. Some tips from the Sandbox Software testing bench:

  • Follow every wire from its battery to its end before you touch anything. Ask: when this is live, where can't I go?
  • Gates remember. Once a gate has had current, it's open for good. You can turn the power off again afterwards, and you usually should.
  • Switches in a row all have to be on for current to get past. Current gets as far as the first switch that is off, so the wire before it is live.
  • Two wires into one gate means either one will do. Pick the one that won't fence you in.
  • One-way trips (diodes, dead batteries, fuses, relays) can't be undone. Do them last, or do them in the right order.
  • Watch the beads. Pulsing current comes in bursts: wait right next to the wire, and roll across just after a burst goes by. You roll exactly as fast as current runs, so you can even ride along right behind a burst.
  • Stuck? Press R to reboot the board. It costs one spare battery, and every board starts exactly as it was.

pages.head: The Boards
pages.html:
The Boards

Twenty-three gadgets in four rooms, from easy to tricky:

RoomBoards
The KitchenThe Toaster, The Blender, The Microwave, The Coffee Maker, The Dishwasher, The Fridge
The Living RoomThe Doorbell, The TV Set, The VCR, The Floor Lamp, The Stereo, The Night-Light
The GarageThe Garage Door Opener, The Wet-Dry Vac, The Power Drill, The Lawn Mower, The Christmas Lights, The CitiCar
The AtticThe Home Computer, The Clock Radio, The Electric Train, The Breadboard Computer, and the main fuse box: Home Sweet Ohm

Between rooms, Watt rides the house wiring to the next one.

pages.head: Registering
pages.html:
Credits and Registering

Ohm Sweet Ohm was designed, drawn, composed and wired by Claude for Sandbox Software, using Game-Maker 3.0 from Recreational Software Designs. No programming was used: every switch, fuse and relay in the game is made of Game-Maker blocks and monsters.

This is shareware

Try it, share it with your friends, upload it to your favorite BBS. If you enjoy Ohm Sweet Ohm, please register for $12. Registered players receive:
